thread.title: TJX: Not On A Special Sale, But A Retailer For The Long Run - TJX Companies Inc. (NYSE:TJX)

author: DoctoRx
title: TJX: Not On A Special Sale, But A Retailer For The Long Run - TJX Companies Inc. (NYSE:TJX)
text:
Introduction - A top-tier company does it again The TJX Companies ( TJX ) reported Q1 earnings for FY 2019 Tuesday morning. TJX is a discounter of apparel and home goods and has an amazing record of success in a brutal field. This is its long-term stock chart:
TJX data by YCharts
Going back to 1987 on Yahoo Finance reveals a 14% CAGR on price, plus dividends, which I estimate brings total return to about 15.5%. Given how brutal retailing has become since the Y2K period - and it never was easy - this is an impressive result. This result compares quite favorably to Walmart ( WMT ):
TJX data by YCharts
So, what is TJX doing right, and what are its prospects?
Q1 results were strong TJX reported a sales gain of 12% and diluted EPS of $1.13. It provided adjusted EPS, thus removing the substantial benefit of December's tax bill, of $0.96, which compares favorably with Q1 2018 EPS of $0.82.
As always, there were some moving parts to each quarter to explain the disproportionate pre-tax PS gain versus the lesser sales gain. Sales of $8.69 B compared favorably to prior year sales of $7.78 B. Currency helped sales by 3% and earnings by $0.04. Selling space rose slightly yoy from 111.7 million gross sq. ft. to 113.1 million.
Management and analysts alike were pleased with the improved in-stock and in-fashion performance of Marmaxx, which is the company's term for its apparel-oriented stores, Marshalls and T.J. Maxx (and related names in many ex-US regions).
Comps were positive in all business segments and all geographic regions.
The company guided for FY 2019 EPS to come in around $4.80.
An extensive capital return program and healthy dividend payouts are anticipated.
The main question is whether TJX can maintain a high P/E. Will its lower tax rate be competed away?
I project that in about a year, TJX can reasonably be projected to trade at a 20X multiple of trailing earnings. Though TJX usually guides conservatively, I'll use the $4.80 number to get to a $96 target by the time Q4 results are in, perhaps March 2019. With TJX having closed Wednesday at $87.89, that suggests about a 9% price gain in about 10 months. Adding in a dividend, that further suggests a 12% total return.
Here's why I think this way and that this is a sustainable total return to expect indefinitely.
TJX has a secret sauce - and it's a secret Last June, the WSJ reported on TJX , and perhaps the key section of the lengthy article reads this way:
The Framingham, Mass., company isn't shifting business online or using big data to figure out what shoppers want. Instead, it has become one of the country's fastest-growing retailers by sticking with a playbook from a vanishing era. It relies heavily on the instincts of its merchandise buyers, many of whom have been with the company for decades. TJX stores rapidly turn over limited quantities of products that are all sold at bargain prices. The result is a rarity in retail - a constant treasure hunt.
"Fresh merchandise hitting the floor is key," said Paul Sweetenham, a former senior executive at TJX's European division. "It's a very simple business model, but it's hard to execute."
Little is known publicly about how the retailer executes its strategy, and TJX declined to make current executives available for interviews.
Interesting commentary. TJX is thriving in the Age of Amazon ( AMZN ):
What I have gleaned from reading several reports from the past 4 years is that like the best category killers including Amazon and Apple ( AAPL ), TJX has a few different core strengths. Meaning, it's not like Walmart or Starbucks ( SBUX ), getting into a space first and using speed, buying power, name recognition, etc. to dominate. Rather, TJX has excelled at marketing , efficient and interest placement of items in stores (creating a "treasure hunt" environment), encouraging word-of-mouth referrals, and perhaps most important, superb purchasing. The company promotes from within and has unusually good relationships with its suppliers. It also has store brands, purchases close-outs from department stores, etc. In a 2014 article, The secret strategy of TJX , it was reported that "many suppliers purposefully create excess merchandise for T.J. Maxx to buy." The article also reported on something that the WSJ emphasized that "TJX buyers spend years perfecting their craft, and go through a rigorous training program."
Years perfecting buying... off-price merchandise? That's something to think about: definitely not the WMT model - nor the deep discount Ross Stores ( ROST ) model.
To summarize this section, TJX has been doing a lot right in rising to its level of success in one of the world's toughest types of business.
Where can, and will, TJX go from here? The Street is looking for $38 B for revenues for TJX this fiscal year, rising to $45 B three years later (FY 2022). That's a 6.1% CAGR. I think that's just a bit conservative, as I expect that the tiny online businesses TJX runs will get more significant. But, working with 6%, and assuming stable margins, financial engineering should add in the range of 1.5% to profits. Adding in the dividend, currently at 1.8%, brings us to a projected EPS growth of 9-10% per year.
The Street is actually projecting 10.8% per share profit growth between 2019 and 2022, so I may be too conservative in that sphere.
In any case, TJX projects significant growth opportunities within the US, partly from Marmaxx and more substantially from HomeGoods and the newly-launched Homesense. It also continues to invest in Sierra Trading Post, both online and with physical stores.
Beyond the US, TJX is the world's most successful discounter focused on apparel and home goods. There is clear, significant growth opportunity within many of TJX's established ex-US regions, which accounted for 23% of sales in Q1. In addition, it's a big world out there, and most people everywhere like a bargain.
Just from growing in established regions, then considering greenfield expansion possibilities, TJX looks like so many other strong chains with something special about it, such as McDonald's ( MCD ) and Starbucks in their years of rapid international growth.
This is key to valuing TJX's stock, because a premium valuation can be justified by durability of growth.
Then there are two other areas of growth to consider. One is vertical expansion. TJX has some of its own lines; these can expand. If it uses a contract manufacturer for them, it can - if it wishes - become its own manufacturer. It can also look into selling more of its store brands, though there are important constraints to that, because part of its appeal is that it sells first-quality branded merchandise at large discounts.
The other is that nothing limits this company to its current fields of apparel and stuff for the house. Two horizontal adjacencies are more stuff for the home and yard, without going so far as to sell lumber, and more stuff for the kitchen, e.g. food.
Over time, business gravitates to the best operators, and currently, few retailers are operating as profitably and with growth characteristics as TJX.
Risks Everything from rising freight rates and labor costs to recession pose a risk to TJX. Strangely, an economic boom diminishes the volume of merchandise it can obtain and sends fewer people to its stores. So in addition to the usual risks, TJX as a business and as a stock has certain other ones.
Everyone wonders about AMZN. So far, the treasure hunt model has insulated TJX from major adverse effects from it. Some of the articles I read in preparing this article found shoppers who use AMZN and like TJX. One point, also, in favor of TJX is that AMZN's physical store efforts are primarily in food, not apparel or goods for the home. Now that AMZN is such a large retailer, sociopolitical and regulatory forces inevitably will be brought to bear to prevent it from swallowing up all effective competition. Thus AMZN is just one of many risks to investing in TJX.
Concluding remarks: TJX for the long run TJX is like AMZN in that it has outlasted countless publicly-traded and privately-held discounters. Its formula has been to provide fashion-fresh items at great discounts. It may now be in an ascendant phase where little can prevent its further growth, both in the US and internationally. This happens to successful companies that emerge from a scrum to dominate their categories and before they have saturated it.
My view of the US and global economy is that they are in pretty good shape, but especially in the US, the Fed tightening always has worked to slow growth, and I expect the same to occur now. This scenario is ideal for TJX, as it allows its costs to be controlled and continues the desire of as many people as possible to put up with an unglamorous shopping experience, and some extra time hunting in the treasure hunt, to save money. I went long TJX in the $85-86 range before earnings due to a combination of the technicals and a desire/need to put some of a very large cash position to work. My one year price target is around $97. Over the years, understanding that eventually all retailers max out, my goal is high-single-digit total returns. Because TJX has strong finances and a strong reputation in a difficult industry, I consider that modest goal as adequate given the known risks.
Note, I am also long ROST, which somehow manages to beat expectations most years and which would also benefit from a slowdown in growth without recession. But I believe that TJX has superior investment characteristics due to more diverse profit streams, both operationally and geographically.
Thanks for reading and sharing any comments you wish to contribute.
Disclosure: I am/we are long TJX, ROST, AAPL.
